# Welcome {.unnumbered}

Postgres is usually introduced as the place where an application keeps its rows. It can also be a
vector store, a job queue, a message broker, the source of a change stream, and the place where
access rules are enforced. Each chapter of this book takes one of those roles and asks what it
costs, and each answer is a measurement.

Everything comes from one repository, [postgres-lab](https://github.com/deburky/postgres-lab). It
holds a set of Docker containers (Postgres 16 and 18 with pgvector and other extensions, a replica,
PgBouncer and Apache Doris), a small FastAPI app that searches the SQLAlchemy documentation, and a
notebook per topic. Every number in the text comes from one of those notebooks, run on a laptop.
The notebooks are in the appendix with their outputs, so you can check any claim against the run
that produced it.

## The map

![](images/world.svg){.column-page .hero fig-alt="An isometric ink drawing of the book as a small world: a Postgres cylinder at the centre of a plate, with five districts around it for Python, Search, Queues, Moving data, and Access and operations."}

::: {.map}
::: {}
**Postgres from Python**

SQLAlchemy sync and async, JSONB documents, PgBouncer, and Postgres in WebAssembly for tests.
:::
::: {}
**Search**

pgvector from four distances to three index types (HNSW, DiskANN, PRISM), and loading vectors fast.
:::
::: {}
**Queues**

Two designs for a queue in a table: pgqueuer's heartbeats and pgmq's visibility timeouts.
:::
::: {}
**Moving data**

Logical replication from one Postgres to another, into Apache Doris with its built-in CDC, and
columnar DuckLake tables inside Postgres itself.
:::
::: {}
**Access and operations**

Roles and grants as code with Pulumi and pgsesame, and the same servers on local Kubernetes.
:::
:::

## How to read it

Each chapter follows the same order. It explains the idea in a few paragraphs, describes the
experiment that tests it, reports what the experiment found, and ends with the traps. The chapters
stand alone, so you can read them in any order. When a chapter mentions "the notebook", it means
the one linked at its end and rendered in the appendix.

Some pages let you try things in the browser. The queue scene above and the vector search scene in
[Chapter 1](chapters/sqlalchemy.qmd) replay traces recorded from the lab's app: real workers, real
`NOTIFY`s and real HNSW searches, played back with no server behind them. The pgvector, JSONB and
pgmq chapters end with a SQL console, a real Postgres running inside the page.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Run it yourself

Clone the repository, then run `cp .env.example .env`, `uv sync` and `just db`. That gives you
Postgres 16 with pgvector on `localhost:5432`, and the notebooks run from there. A few need a second
server, which their chapter names. [Running the lab](chapters/running-the-lab.qmd) has the details.
:::
